### Choose what to teach by its leverage

Choose what knowledge to teach by its leverage (how often later texts and tests draw on it, what builds on it and how widely it transfers). Frequency kept a 25% weight, only as a sanity check that makes every high-leverage outlier be defended.

The reading project's topic selection for a Grade 3 course weights a reasoned leverage score at 0.75 and keeps frequency, how many of 7 expert programs teach the topic, at 25% as an external sanity check, because what the field commonly teaches is other people's design choices, not a discovered structure (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g3-reading/iteration-2/approval-package-v2/sources/TOPIC-SELECTION.md`). In its worked examples the most frequently taught candidate had the lowest leverage and was rejected, and student interest was struck as a ground for keeping a topic because it tested flat as a learning driver (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g3-reading/iteration-2/approval-package-v2/sources/LOAD-BEARING-METRIC.md`). Use how commonly others teach a topic only as a minor check, and don't count how interesting it seems.

### Cite each block by a fixed label

Give every block a short label that is never renumbered or reused, name every automatic finding by it, and show the labels beside any page that carries none.

The lesson engine's composer gives each block a code and a number, keeps the highest number ever given per code, and never renumbers or reuses one (`g9/transformer/web/app.js`). Its playtest names every engine finding by the block's label (`g9/transformer/src/server.js`), and because the players' own pages carry no labels, a line over the frame names the blocks they are showing. The engine's own lesson view prints each label on the page (`g9/transformer/web/lesson.js`), and its decisions ask for a short identifier on every block to cite (`g9/transformer/DECISIONS.md`).

### Claim no more than the evidence

Before a study becomes a design rule, check its learners, task and contrast, say how strong its evidence is, and read its effect size as a direction only. One review warned against predicting, for Grade 3 learners, the g=.66 a meta-analysis found for prequestioned information.

A review of the research behind an outside content review (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-devfactory-2026-09-10/analysis-current-courses/RESEARCH-BOUNDARIES.md`, 2026-09-10) checked three clusters against the primary papers and found that a mandatory visible mascot cue, a universal after-reading-only rule and claims on feedback timing and size exceeded the evidence; it labels its own design conclusions inferences for evaluation. An adversarial critique of a course-improvement dossier found effect sizes from general, mixed-age literature listed beside planned changes and asked for a direction-not-magnitude tag wherever one appears (`grade3-reading/artifacts/alpha-read-packager/v2_final_package/docs/V2_MONSTER_DOSSIER.md`). A closing-questions design carries an evidence-status table so that nothing in it is defended on a stronger basis than it deserves, rating retrieval and fading well evidenced, SOLO and threshold concepts frameworks, and choral repetition weak (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-closing-questions-2026-09-24/Closing_Questions_Pattern.txt`). An effect size found elsewhere is not a forecast for your own learners.

### Clear the rights before building

Clear the rights to every text, clip and image before building on it, since viewing rights don't cover excerpts and a withdrawn text takes everything built on it.

For a Grade 9 plan to compare two stage productions, every published licence found granted platform viewing, not clip extraction or embedding in another app, so each holder needed a direct rights conversation, with a text-only comparison as the fallback (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0202-g9-othello-video-research-fake-ai-attention.qmd`). The edition chosen for the text is free for non-commercial use, with attribution and a link to the licence required (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0251-g9-prep-pack-index-manifests-leadership-playbook.qmd`). In the reading project, teaching materials offered in a meeting were leads, not a licence: receipt, rights and permitted use are confirmed before any goes into a training corpus (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0172-g3-reading-course-feedback-2026-08-04.qmd`).

### Close the class, not the instance

Treat each defect, finding or failure as a class: repair its kind and add a standing check across everything made the same way, not just the items that failed. 39 checks were added in 5 weeks, yet one defect class took seven separate commits.

The reading project's QA notes found that 39 checks were added in 5 weeks (7-10 a week) while the same defect classes kept coming back, one of them across seven separate commits, and a later formatting commit silently reverted an earlier pronunciation fix. What converged was closing a finding only when its whole class has an executable check of what the student experiences, and counting new against repeat classes in every round report. When one instance of a text-to-speech trap turned up, the rule became a census of every instance in the course file rather than assuming a one-off, and a give-away cue rule was swept over every grade. Where code can't check a class, a dated rule stands in for the check, and each check is shown to fire before the fix and runs on every lesson.

### Code gates catch broken items, not weak ones

Hard-block in code only what code detects reliably, keep keyword and length counts advisory, and check quality and correctness separately, since a well-formed item can be weak or wrong. A deterministic suite caught 19 of 102 failing items and rejected 22 of 351 passing ones.

On 30 scored AP question sets, a stage validator passed 12 of the 14 failing sets and wrongly failed 1 of the 16 passing ones, and its results note concluded that hard gates are a safety layer, not a quality judge, since most failures were semantic rather than schema or leak failures. Its first version also hard-blocked reading-style, source-referential stems and over-blocked known passing items, so the split kept hard gates for schema, missing fields, answer leaks, extreme length and key clustering and made wording flags advisory. A separate probe of a deterministic suite on 461 generated items caught 19 of 102 failures and rejected 22 of 351 passes, and a shape-only acceptance test passed 25 of 25 in 0.006 s while a graded retest of the same service scored 8 of 20. Code gates catch broken items, not weak ones. Keyword and wording counts stay advisory, as does length unless it is extreme, since a valid shape does not show quality.

### Compare failure overlaps with chance

Compare the overlap between two runs' failures with chance before reading it as a pattern, because when both runs fail most items many shared failures are forced. 36 of 58 items failed in both runs, but with 42 and at least 48 failures among those items at least 32 had to overlap, and chance alone gives about 35.

Two AP models trained by very different methods were scored on the same 58 document-based items, and 36 failed under both; the note read this as proof that the same items fail whatever the method (`icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_dbq_floor_is_data_veracity.md`, lines 17-37). One model passed 16 of 58 and the other 10 of 60, so at least 32 shared failures were forced and independent runs would share about 34.8 to 36.2. The overlap was no better than chance, and the note never made that comparison.

### Compare like reliability with like

Compare a reliability figure only with the same kind of reliability measured under like conditions, because one test's marginal, test-retest and sub-score reliabilities can differ markedly. One reference test reported 0.96 marginal reliability on its calibrated pool, 0.82–0.89 test-retest and 0.87–0.88 for its sub-scores.

An adversarial review set a proxy test's simulated reliability of 0.931 against the reference test's operational 0.96. The package's reply cited the reference test's technical report for 2024–25: the 0.96 is marginal reliability of the operational adaptive test on a fully calibrated pool, its test-retest reliability across terms is 0.82–0.89, and its sub-scores average 0.87–0.88. It called holding a pre-calibration simulation to the operational-pool figure a category error, and its simulation evidence names 0.96 after calibration, not before, as the comparison to hold it to.

### Compare on the same frozen mix

Compare runs only on the same frozen items, mix and checks, or else type by type, because a shift in mix or difficulty moves the numbers by itself. One essay type passed 99.3% in a run with none of one unit's requests and 90.0% in a run made only of them, which its notes call a test distribution change, not a code regression.

In one generator's notes, an essay type's pass rate fell from 99.3% to 90.0% because the second run was made entirely of one unit's requests, whose time period clashed with their topics; the notes call it a test distribution change, not a regression. A 12-item mini run scored 100% while the 116-item run scored 50.0%, because the mini run never checked cognitive demand. A training note declined to compare against results from older checker versions, since that would conflate rubric drift with model drift. The mix means the topics, item types and levels, and the checks include the checker's version. A changed baseline, such as new standards, also moves the numbers by itself.

### Correlation is not agreement

Judge whether one measure, such as a model marker, can replace another by how far and which way individual scores differ, not by correlation, which misses a uniformly generous marker. In one simulation, two item banks' scores for the same students correlated at 0.902 yet had 95% limits of agreement of −11.4 to +11.1 points.

A reading assessment's simulation scored the same 2,000 simulated students on its own bank and on a synthetic bank modelled on the reference test's pool, using the standard method-comparison approach: the two scores correlated at 0.902, but the 95% limits of agreement ran from −11.4 to +11.1 points. Its authoritative later run gave 0.918 with limits of −10.0 to +10.0. The package also notes that its ability-recovery correlation of 0.948 measures ranking accuracy, not absolute accuracy.

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/03_SIMULATION_EVIDENCE.md` (235): “| Correlation (r) | **0.902** | Strong agreement in ranking |”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/03_SIMULATION_EVIDENCE.md` (238): “| 95% Limits of Agreement | **[−11.4, +11.1] RIT** | Individual scores may differ by up to ±11 RIT |”

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/03_SIMULATION_EVIDENCE.md` (21): “**0.918 / [−10.0, +10.0] RIT** | r ≥ 0.85 |”

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g4g5-writing/approval-package/sources/CALIBRATION-HARNESS-SPEC.md` (57-59): “predicts the LLM is **systematically too generous, and a bigger model makes it worse** — **a 0.8 correlation with a +0.7-band offset is a broken scorer.** Report false-high (safety- critical: a weak response scored 2) separately from false-low”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g4g5-writing/approval-package/sources/CALIBRATION-HARNESS-SPEC.md` (55): “**Agreement report — the SIGNED gap, not just correlation.**”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g4g5-writing/approval-package/sources/CALIBRATION-HARNESS-SPEC.md` (102): “**87.5% agreement (42/48), 1 false-high, 0 concerning**”

Published: [Statistical methods for assessing agreement between two methods of clinical measurement (The Lancet, 1986)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(86)90837-8)

Against: The second bank was synthetic, so this measures the engine's internal consistency, not agreement with the real test: "It is emphatically not a measurement of agreement with NWEA MAP — the comparison bank is synthetic." (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/03_SIMULATION_EVIDENCE.md`, line 220). The narrower band expected after linking is "a hope stated in advance, not a result" (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/04_CONCURRENT_VALIDITY_PLAN.md`, line 25). The generosity is a prediction carried over from research on estimating item difficulty, not a measurement of this marker, and the harness makes no certification claim until a real gold set replaces its synthetic seed (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g4g5-writing/approval-package/sources/CALIBRATION-HARNESS-SPEC.md`, lines 122-123).

### Cost a per-learner model trigger

Trigger a full worked model the first time each learner meets each procedure at each stage, tracked per learner rather than by date, and cost that trigger before building. In one design, a learner who climbs every stage could meet up to 36 compulsory models across roughly 96 lessons.

A Grade 3 reading lesson design gives a child a compulsory full model the first time they meet a stage, and because its stages are available rather than assigned, that first time is a per-child event, not a date in the scheme (`g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx`, line 40). So the app has to hold a per-child matrix of procedure by stage and fire the full model on each cell the first time it is entered (line 41). Nine procedures by four stages make 36 cells, so a child who climbs all four stages could meet up to 36 compulsory models across roughly 96 lessons, more than a third of them on the long path, a cost the design says is worth knowing before it is built.

Quoted:

- `g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx` (40): “The rule is that a child gets a compulsory full model the FIRST time they meet a stage.”
- `g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx` (40): “If stages are available rather than assigned, that first time is a per-child event, not a date in the scheme.”
- `g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx` (41): “So the app has to hold a per-child matrix of procedure by stage, and fire the full model on each cell the first time it is entered.”
- `g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx` (41): “Nine rails by four stages is 36 cells. A child who climbs all four stages could meet up to 36 compulsory models across roughly 96 lessons, which is more than a third of them running the long path.”
- `g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx` (41): “That is the real cost of making stages available, and it is worth knowing before it is built rather than after.”

Against: none found

### Cost every path against the time window

Cost every path through an adaptive lesson against its accepted time window before building, and when shedding optional parts can't fit a path, change the scheme, not the protected parts. One design's ~900-word lesson with a full model runs to 31:00 against a 29-minute ceiling and cannot be shed back under it.

A Grade 3 reading lesson design checks every time in it against an accepted 22 to 29 minute window (`g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx`, line 2). One path, a ~900-word text with a full model, runs to 31:00 and cannot be shed back under 29, because there is nothing left to shed (lines 108-110 and 453). The design treats the remedy, shorter texts in the back third of the year or a split lesson, as a scheme decision rather than a lesson-design one, and never trades the read-aloud, the comprehension checks, the taught word, the modelled write-up or the independent write (lines 111, 453 and 454).

- `g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx` (453): “The 900-word lesson with a full model gets 8:40 and cannot be rescued by shedding, because there is nothing left to shed.”
- `g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx` (454): “The practical consequence is a text-length constraint on the back third of the year, which is a scheme decision rather than a lesson-design one.”
- `g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx` (111): “What is never traded: the read-aloud, the comprehension checks, the taught word, step 4 of the Modelling Moment, and Part 3.”

### Count only independent agreement

Treat a finding as settled only when independent methods or sources reach it. One faulty item was caught both by a blind solve that guessed it 4 times out of 4 and by a separate reading of its options' length and phrasing.

A review of 269 teaching-video transcripts, split into 9 batches, treated findings that recurred across independent batches as high-confidence and a technique seen once as a candidate, not a rule (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/IES-CORPUS-REVIEW-2026-08-05.md`, lines 13-18). In one build, two agents grepped a file holding a NUL byte without the flag that reads such files, both got nothing, and both reported that no filter existed: true, as it turned out, but reached by an invalid method twice (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g3-reading/iteration-3/BUILD-RULES.md`, lines 1104-1117). A red-team addendum calls two independent instruments landing on one item the strongest signal in the document, and the argument for running both. A finding seen once, carried from another project, or reached twice by the same source, model or method is a single candidate.

### Count the learners who were there

Compute an outcome rate over the learners actually enrolled, from one consistent measure, and follow the same learners over time. Averaged over every student in the network, one course's completion read 0.007; counting only enrolled students and the app's own measure, it was 0.707.

An audit of a low-completion finding for second-grade reading ruled the headline numbers ~90% measurement artifact: the report view held one row per active student in the network, 18,359, of whom 140 were enrolled, and it mixed the app's bounded progress with an unbounded fallback, so the course that looked catastrophic at 0.007 had the highest average completion of its group, 0.707, once only enrolled students and the app's own measure were counted (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/dropout-3-data-integrity.md`). A red-team pass on the grade's reading data found a cross-grade slide of 77 to 50 to 45 to be a Simpson's-paradox artifact of which campuses entered the sample in which season: within one season there was no slide, and current students tested twice rose 7.8 percentile points (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/redteam-1-data-integrity.md`). A wrong denominator or a changing mix of learners manufactures failures and declines.

### Count unique certified items

Count banks and rates by distinct, independently certified items per type, not rows, which hide repeats, treating an item's variants as that item and keeping them in one split. One bank of 143,026 rows held 49,571 unique candidates and 0 independently certified ones.

An inventory of the AP history question substrate found 143,026 gross rows, 49,571 sampling-eligible unique candidate bodies and 0 independently certified rows, so a claim of 100,000 usable items was rejected (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0170-apush-deliverable-shape-user-pause-checkpoint.qmd`). Its deterministic split kept 606 lineage-connected groups whole, with zero collisions across strata, and its remaining work includes rejecting contamination between training, development and audit sets. Every variant of one item, its paraphrases, number swaps and shared templates, is kept in the same split.

### Count visible support before calling it missing

Before a review calls a lesson's support missing, count the choices, labels, captions and images on screen, and judge only what is needed at that moment.

The method written for the simulated outside review in a Grade 5 lesson preflight tells it to count choices, labels, captions and images as visible learner information before claiming support is absent, and to judge information at its point of need rather than demand the passage during a self-contained pre-reading step. It also reacts to the visible journey before reading any implementation evidence. The rules were written for that one simulated character; nothing cited shows them applied to people reviewing a lesson.

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/quality/adversarial-preflight/characters/external-instructional-reviewer/character.json` (10): “Count choices, labels, captions, and images as visible learner information before claiming support is absent.”
- `grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/quality/adversarial-preflight/characters/external-instructional-reviewer/character.json` (9): “Judge information at its point of need; do not demand the passage during a self-contained pre-reading action.”
- `grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/quality/adversarial-preflight/characters/external-instructional-reviewer/character.json` (7): “React to the visible journey before reading any implementation evidence.”

Against: The rules were written for one simulated outside review in a lesson preflight, and nothing cited shows them applied when people review a lesson.

### Count what was checked, not what was filled

Count what was checked, not what was filled: a populated answer, score or 'verified' field says nothing about whether the content is right or whether anyone reviewed it. One report on 4,165 extracted questions turned an answer field filled for 99.7% of them into a claim that 99.7% have correct answers.

A report on 4,165 questions extracted from 1,993 PDF resources presented field population as quality: an answer field filled for 99.7% of questions became "99.7% have correct answers", and the summary claimed 99.9%+ accuracy in core educational data (`icloud-work/incept/input-generator/UAE_EDUCATIONAL_ANALYSIS_FINAL_REPORT.md`). Its human-verified field was 100% populated although the schema gives it a default of false, so the count shows a filled field, not a review.

### Credit what works, specifically

Name what works in a lesson, specifically, as well as what fails, because an audit that concedes nothing reads as rhetoric.

The reading course's agent spec lists conceding genuine strengths up front among its red-team agent's lessons from rejected work, since an audit that concedes nothing reads as rhetoric (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/course-formula-agents.md`, line 172). Its quality gates' operating rules end on the same point: credit what is good, specifically (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/key-quality-gates.md`, line 154). Both are adopted rules; neither records a measured effect.

### Cut repeats before content

When a lesson feels long, cut its redundant repeats, such as an answer shown twice, before any content, but keep deliberate returns like a framing line. One prototype lesson showed its learning question three times.

A review of a Grade 9 lesson prototype counted its repeats: the same six words introduced on two screens, the learning question three times and the answer twice. It judged each one small, but together a large part of why the lesson felt long, and cutting them cheaper than cutting content. Its checklist made an audit for repeated content, and explaining the program once at first open instead of again in every unit, priority items. The unit's film script kept a statement made in both its first and eighth scenes, calling it a frame, not the repetition the review objected to (`g9/library/text/L5d411f.txt`, line 23).

Quoted:

- `g9/sources/Othello_1_Feedback_DevFactory.md` (30): “Two screens introduce the same six words. The Learning Question appears three times. The answer is shown twice.”
- `g9/sources/Othello_1_Feedback_DevFactory.md` (30): “Each instance is small; together they are a large part of why the lesson feels long, and cutting them is cheaper than cutting content.”
- `g9/sources/Othello_1_Feedback_DevFactory.md` (57): “Explain the program once, at first open. Remove the per-unit re-explanation of how the program works.”
- `g9/sources/Othello_1_Feedback_DevFactory.md` (130): “Audit the lesson for repeated content: the six words twice, the Learning Question three times, the answer twice.”
- `g9/library/text/L36b8ba.txt` (30): “Two screens introduce the same six words. The Learning Question appears three times. The answer is shown twice.”
- `g9/library/text/L36b8ba.txt` (30): “Each instance is small; together they are a large part of why the lesson feels long, and cutting them is cheaper than cutting content.”
- `g9/library/text/L36b8ba.txt` (130): “Audit the lesson for repeated content: the six words twice, the Learning Question three times, the answer twice.”
- `g9/library/text/L5d411f.txt` (23): “Scene 1 and scene 8 both state love → murder: a frame, not the repetition she objects to.”

Against: The same review separates a lesson that is long from one that only feels long: "Twenty-eight steps each doing distinct work is a session-length decision. Twenty-eight where several feel similar is redundancy, and the fix is cutting or merging" (`g9/sources/Othello_1_Feedback_DevFactory.md`, line 202). Cutting repeats answers a lesson that feels long, not one that is long.

### Decide first, then regenerate once

Settle the decisions that change what content must be, such as its target level, before regenerating anything, then fold every fix into one gated regeneration. One remediation plan refused to regenerate 75 passages before deciding whether the course was meant to be at grade level, and the decision it recorded needed no passage rebuild.

A grade-6 reading course's remediation plan, written after an adversarial review, ordered its work by dependency and leverage rather than severity: two critical findings were decisions, not builds, and they gated the costly content work (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g6-reading/G6-REMEDIATION-SEQUENCE.md`, lines 4-6). Because raising the reading level forces passage regeneration and the items are tied to their passages, it folded every content fix into one gated regeneration rather than re-shipping the items five times (lines 39-41). The decision recorded afterwards, following a recheck of the reading-level estimate, found the texts already at band, so the build needed no passage rebuild (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g6-reading/G6-FORK-DECISION.md`, lines 14 and 16).

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g6-reading/G6-REMEDIATION-SEQUENCE.md` (4-6): “**Ordering principle:** dependencies + leverage, not raw severity. Two Criticals are *decisions*, not builds, and they gate the expensive content work. Do not regenerate 75 passages before deciding whether the course is even meant to be at grade level.”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g6-reading/G6-REMEDIATION-SEQUENCE.md` (39-41): “because raising it forces passage regeneration and items are passage-linked, bake EVERYTHING into one gated regen rather than re-shipping items 5×:”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g6-reading/G6-FORK-DECISION.md` (16): “What this means for the build (post-Lexile-recheck: all cheap, no passage rebuild)”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g6-reading/G6-FORK-DECISION.md` (14): “Keep the grade-6 mastery claim — the text is already at band (consensus 1020L), so it's honest.”

Against: It rests on one plan, and the five-fold re-ship it avoided is the plan's own projection, not a measured cost.

### Declare what each assessment is for

Before judging a course or assessment, declare its purpose (teaching, practice, mastery gate, diagnostic), judge it by that alone, and set pass marks only on checks that gate progress. One course keeps its 24-item mastery gate, set at 90%, apart from a growth test that has no 90% threshold and gates nothing.

The assessment packet has the product type declared first, as formative, mastery, diagnostic, summative or cold measurement, and bars calling a diagnostic score a grade, since diagnostics route study under uncertainty (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/handoffs/g3-reading-v2-feedback-2026-07-16/assessment-item-agent.md`). A course validator fails a check-bearing screen that declares no product type, because the type decides which criteria apply (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/handoffs/g3-reading-v2-feedback-2026-07-16/tooling/ti-courseplans-2169d1f/docs/standards/course-json/tools/course_validate.py`), and the evaluator gap list names the same declaration (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0093-evaluator-gap-analysis-inceptbench-academics-2026-07-09.qmd`). The course checklist and the staged assessment standard keep the 24-item mastery gate apart from the growth measure, which uses cold passages, scores raw out of 40 with a band and is never gated on, and they call its predictive claim a design intent until a linking study runs (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/CHECKLIST.md`, `grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/pr-proposals/ti-courseplans-standards/staged/docs/standards/assessment-design.md`). The purposes also include placement, a final summary and a transfer measure on unseen material, and the declaration should come with the assessment's full specification. Pass marks belong only on checks that decide progress.

### Design the experience before the interface

Design what students will see, hear, examine and think about before the interface, and make the interface serve that experience rather than varying layouts without it. All five layout drafts, each of which had passed its interaction checks, were rejected in review.

Five alternative layouts for the Grade 9 unit's app passed their interaction checks, with visual browser checks still unverified (`g9/transcript/chat-transcript.redacted.txt`, lines 4944-4946), and when asked to pick one, review rejected all five (lines 5368 and 5397). Later builds drew the same complaint (line 6733). The direction was then reset to the experience described, a mature illustrated-book experience with rich scenes worth examining, compelling narration, quiet optional help and space for students to think, with the interface serving it (line 6754), and the reset was endorsed (line 6775).

### Difficulty levels that don't overlap

Define a standard's difficulty levels so they don't overlap, and check that every learning objective still maps to at least one of them.

The curriculum review skill lists reworking a standard's difficulty definitions so that easy, medium and hard partition the input space as a recurring kind of change, approved if every learning objective still maps to a tier. The evaluator relies on these definitions: when none are provided, its base rules tell the judge not to fail difficulty on its own judgment and to score it 1.0.

Quoted:

- `shadow-curriculum/.agents/skills/curriculum-pr-review/SKILL.md` (46): “| **Disjoint difficulty tiers** | Reworks `difficulty_definitions` so easy/medium/hard partition the input space | **Approve** if every learning objective still maps to a tier |”
- `shadow-bench/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/_base_evaluation.txt` (35): “Failing `difficulty_alignment` using your own judgment when no curriculum difficulty definitions are provided. Without definitions → 1.0.”

Against: One row of a review table, with no measurement behind it.

### Disambiguate a rule that reads two ways

When a content rule can be read two ways, add a one-line disambiguation and an example of what it does and doesn't forbid. In an audit against 325 rules, one rule read the wrong way would have made every card of one kind in the shipped course defective.

A Grade 3 lesson was audited against a nine-document rulebook, 325 rules in all, by nine independent rule-by-rule audits, an adversarial pass on every serious finding and a re-check of each one that survived. One rule, that a vocabulary card's example never contains the target word, was read by a careful audit as never containing the word being defined, which would have made every card of that kind in the shipped course defective; the intended meaning was another card's taught word. The verdict counted it among four problems in the rulebook itself and asked for a one-line disambiguation with an example.

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/artifacts/l4-audit/VERDICT.md` (344-346): “04 §3's *"The example never contains the target word"* was read by a careful auditor as *"never contains the word being defined"* — which would make **every V3 card in the shipped course** defective.”
- `grade3-reading/artifacts/l4-audit/VERDICT.md` (346-347): “This needs a one-line disambiguation and an example”

Against: none found

### Don't rehearse the test you validate against

When validating a new measure against an established test, don't let it act as practice for that test. In one validation plan about half the cohort sits the official test first, which gives a linking estimate with no prior exposure to the new test.

An adversarial review of a reading assessment's validity plan pointed out that giving the new test days before the official one would be a practice intervention on the very test it was being validated against (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/RED_TEAM_FINDINGS.md`). The plan has every student take both tests within two weeks in counterbalanced order, so the half that sits the official test first gives a linking estimate with no prior exposure, and it offers an arm that gives the new test only after the official sitting (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/04_CONCURRENT_VALIDITY_PLAN.md`). Counterbalancing measures the practice effect rather than removing it, so the plan reports the official-score difference between the two orders as a study output. The retest literature it cites puts practice effects at about d = 0.24 to 0.26 per re-administration, and it expects format familiarity without item overlap to sit well below that.

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/RED_TEAM_FINDINGS.md` (21): “rehearsal administered days before the real test is a **practice/familiarization intervention on the criterion measure**”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/04_CONCURRENT_VALIDITY_PLAN.md` (65): “All students take both tests (within 2 weeks). Order is counterbalanced to control for practice effects and fatigue:”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/04_CONCURRENT_VALIDITY_PLAN.md` (81): “Group B (MAP-first, ~50% of the cohort) provides a linking estimate with zero prior proxy exposure by construction.”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/04_CONCURRENT_VALIDITY_PLAN.md` (81): “The Group A vs Group B official-MAP score difference is reported as an explicit study output: it directly estimates any practice effect of a proxy sitting on the official score”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/04_CONCURRENT_VALIDITY_PLAN.md` (81): “d ≈ 0.24–0.26 per re-administration, Hausknecht et al. 2007”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/04_CONCURRENT_VALIDITY_PLAN.md` (81): “a **post-MAP-only administration arm** is available: the proxy administered only after the official sitting.”
- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/RED_TEAM_RESPONSE.md` (5): “three of its load-bearing findings rest on factual errors — a counterbalancing design it says doesn't exist”

### Every activity states its rationale

Before an activity goes in, write its rationale: the knowledge and performance it targets, the failure it guards against, why this activity, and when its support comes off.

The general instruction rules a second-round review applied to the reading course say any activity needs a rationale: the target knowledge type, the performance, the failure mode it protects against, why this activity, and the condition for retiring its scaffold. The reading project's lesson-plan validator checks that every assessment item argues its format.

### Every count from one dated pull

Keep every count, figure, rule and setting in one named, dated, re-runnable source, and derive every document and copy from it rather than editing each by hand. One course's email said 52 lessons and 745 items and its infographic 47 lessons and 713, all citing one data pull.

An outside review of the reading project's first course found its own materials disagreeing on lesson and item counts, though all of them cited the same data pull dated 18 June 2026 (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0081-g3-reviewer-feedback-raw-2026-07-02-reading-explorers-v2-review-verbatim.qmd`). The next course's rule was that every count in every document traces to one named pull with a date, with a render-truth manifest as the one source (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0236-g5-package-build-facts-and-g3-fixlist-apply-2026-07-02.qmd`). A consistency linter for stale numbers helped but was not enough: stragglers survived green runs, so a broad search followed it, and downstream counts were recomputed after every fix wave (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0089-parent-claude-sessions-worklog-2026-07-09.qmd`). Errors are fixed in the one source and counts recomputed after each fix, and no number is carried over from another group or slice.

### Every field a student meets is checked

Make sure every field a student sees or hears is read by at least one check. Three clips played as silence behind a passing build because no check looked for them.

In one course nothing validated the lesson-page video checkpoints and nothing checked that voice-over clips existed, and three clips played as silence behind a green build until both checks were added (`grade3-reading/artifacts/DECISIONS-2026-08-24.md`). Review clips carried no hash of the text they voice, so a definition edit left a clip silently stale (`grade3-reading/artifacts/l4-p3-stale-clip-2026-09-29/README.md`), and the audit script never read the search fields at all, the direct root cause of a leak in those fields that no machine caught (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-inceptbench-2026-09-30/REGISTER.md`).

### Every targeted misconception can surface

Check that every misconception a lesson means to catch is keyed by a wrong option or judged answer and routed to its own feedback, or it goes undetected. A full-file search found three misconception ids in one lesson's content, none of them the one the lesson existed to catch.

An audit of a Grade 5 lesson searched its whole content file and found that the misconception the lesson existed to catch, trusting only one of its two sources, had no wrong option keyed to it, no feedback routed to it and no id anywhere, while three other misconception ids were present. The fix added a wrong option keyed to it with its own scaffolding feedback, and later verification found it routed live through that option. The gap was found by a full-file search for the misconception's id.

### Evidence of the kind the claim makes

Accept a claim only on evidence of its kind, runtime evidence for behaviour, independent review of the exact text for meaning, access testing for access, however much weaker evidence agrees.

The student-course quality standard asks of every requirement verdict whether the evidence type matches the claim: runtime claims use runtime evidence, semantic claims independent semantic review, access claims access testing, and state and event claims a reconciliation of recorded behaviour (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/quality/golden-student-course/versions/1.0.0/STANDARD.qmd`, lines 97-102). Its failure signals are static prose used for runtime behaviour, self-review used as independent judgment and screenshots used for accessibility, and it holds that a weaker evidence type cannot be upgraded by confidence or repetition (lines 103-104). The Grade 5 instruction-review profile applies it: presentation claims need runtime evidence because source files or tests alone cannot prove them, and semantic claims need the exact learner-facing text in context (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/courses/g5-reading/review/generated/instruction-review-profile.json`, lines 154-155).

- `grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/quality/golden-student-course/versions/1.0.0/STANDARD.qmd` (102): “Runtime claims use runtime evidence; semantic claims use independent semantic review; access claims use access testing;”

### Examples must obey their rules

Every example in a standard's description must obey the rules beside it; when a rule and its example disagree, decide which is the source of truth and fix the other. A rule that one or more digits must be 0 sat beside an example of 40.271, so the rule was dropped and the example kept as the source of truth.

The curriculum review skill names rule-versus-example consistency as a recurring kind of change: a rule clause that contradicts an example in the same entry, such as 'must be 2-digit' beside an example of 5.03, is removed when the examples are the documented source of truth. A rewrite of difficulty content is read carefully to verify that the examples don't violate the rules they sit next to. The skill records these as calls that needed human judgement in real reviews.

Quoted:

- `shadow-curriculum/.agents/skills/curriculum-pr-review/SKILL.md` (45): “| **Rule-vs-example consistency** | Removes a rule clause that contradicts an in-leaf example (e.g. "must be 2-digit" but example is `5.03`) | **Approve** if examples are the documented source of truth |”

### Exemptions leave with what they exempt

Have a check fail on any exemption or known-fault entry that nothing current matches. When branch replies landed in all 18 lessons, the check went red until its two now-fixed known-flat entries were deleted.

In a Grade 3 reading build, a drift check exempted beats by label, and a second exemption, added the morning a new beat shipped, was dropped the same evening when that beat was removed: kept, it would have waved any later beat with that label through unexamined, so the rulebook holds that an exemption exists only for a label something currently produces and leaves with that label. The build keeps replies that are still flat in a named deferral table that may only shrink, since an assertion checks that every row is still flat: when branch replies landed in all 18 lessons, the gate went red until the two fixed rows were deleted, so a fixed defect became a required edit rather than a stale note. When image descriptions were reclassed as phrases, exempt from a sentence test, a doubled word planted inside the newly exempted text still failed, so the exemption did not become a silencer. A second learning from the same rulebook is kept here rather than in the statement: plant a fault inside each exemption to show that real faults there still fail, which the rulebook calls the check any exemption owes.

### Feed every ruling back to the checker

When a flagged item is ruled fine, record the ruling where the checker reads it, so the same false flag doesn't come back on later runs.

The content audit for Grade 3 reading lessons decides which unfamiliar words to flag from a grade-3 known-word list. Each time a lesson is adjudicated, a word found to be known is added there, which silences its false flags on every later run, and the audit's notes call the list accumulated judgment, not a static config (`shadow/content-eval/README.md`).

### Feedback rules only its own course

Treat feedback on one course as a ruling for that course only, and check each point against another course's build before carrying it over. Four complaints about a Grade 3 build did not apply to the Grade 5 build, which already handled them, while one more, a passive modelling phase, did.

A reading-lesson project's standing rules scope feedback to the course it was given on and say that a matching string in another course is not a ruling. When feedback raised on a Grade 3 build was checked against the Grade 5 build, four complaints (sentence starters, feedback that restates instead of evaluating, minimum-word limits that force padding, and telling the student what to type) did not apply, because the Grade 5 build already handled them. A fifth, that the modelling phase gives the student nothing to do, did carry over.

- `grade3-reading/curriculum-gen/.agent/AGENT.md` (125-126): “**Reviewer feedback is scoped to its own course.** A matching string elsewhere is not a ruling.”

### Find story words by their concentration

To catch a question that needs a story detail not yet read, track only words concentrated in at most two of the collection's texts, measured from the texts themselves.

A forward-reference checker for Grade 3 narrative lessons flags a question, option, hint or feedback line that depends on a concrete story noun the child has not read yet. It builds a document-frequency table over every lesson's passages, so a word found across many stories counts as general vocabulary and only words concentrated in one or two stories are tracked, measured from the file rather than a hand-written list. It skips the preview pages before a lesson's first passage, which were its largest source of false alarms on approved lessons.

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/curriculum-gen/checks/check-forward-reference.mjs` (5-7): “A question, option, feedback or hint on page N must not depend on a concrete story noun the child has not read yet: one whose first passage appearance is on a page AFTER N, or which appears in no passage of the lesson at all.”

### Find what every run shared

When many runs agree on a limit, find what they all had in common before calling it a limit. Retrained on the same data with only its learning rate corrected, one multiple-choice item type went from 76.7% to 93.3%.

Across eleven training runs every useful variant landed between 76.7% and 85.0%, and the band was recorded as the model's ceiling (`icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_14b_saturation.md`). All of them had been trained with a learning rate set far too low (`icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_lr_was_too_low.md`), and the project's memory rules now list "All 11 experiments saw X, so X is a law." among the patterns to refuse until shared confounds are checked (`icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/MEMORY_GOVERNANCE.md`). Retrained on the same data with the rate corrected, two multiple-choice item types went from 80.0% to 90.0% and from 76.7% to 93.3% (`icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_v20a_lr1e4_result.md`).

Quoted:

- `icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/MEMORY_GOVERNANCE.md` (113): “- **"All 11 experiments saw X, so X is a law."** → no. Check the shared confounds (e.g., wrong LR across all 11).”
- `icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_lr_was_too_low.md` (24): “**v8/v18/v9/v11/v12/v13d/v14a/v15/v16b/v17 all used LR 2e-5.** All experiments tonight are confounded by this mistake.”
- `icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_14b_saturation.md` (15): “The pattern band is tight: every "useful" variant lands in [76.7%, 85.0%] aggregate.”
- `icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_v20a_lr1e4_result.md` (25): “| apush/mcq | 80.0% (0.902) | **90.0%** (0.941) | +10.0pp |”
- `icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_v20a_lr1e4_result.md` (30): “| apwh/mcq | 76.7% (0.894) | **93.3%** (0.925) | +16.6pp |”

Against: The fix did not lift everything: "| apush/mcq_set | 50.0% (0.862) | 36.7% (0.699) | **−13.3pp** |" (`icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_v20a_lr1e4_result.md`, line 26). The band came from runs scored on 60 multiple-choice prompts and mostly trained on multiple-choice items only, while the corrected run was trained on all types. ### Find why completion is low first

Before blaming content for low completion, check when learners started, how accurate they were before stopping and how long the course is against the time they had. In one grade, 69% of the learners who did little work had started only in the last six weeks of the year.

Dropout analyses of a second-grade reading cohort found non-completion driven by timing rather than content: 87 of 126 minimal-work learners (69%) logged their first activity only in the last six weeks of the year, and about 13% were genuine quitters (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/dropout-4-who.md`, line 16; `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/g2-completion-and-course-findings.md`, lines 84-85). There was no frustration cliff: accuracy held near 75% up to the last activity before a learner stopped, and the early accuracy of those who abandoned was within about 8 points of completers' (the same two files, lines 82-83 and 18). A headline contrast of 12.5% against about 88% completion was an artifact of course length: the short courses marked learners complete after trivial work, while the main course's denominator was 30 times larger and too long to finish in a year at the observed pace (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/dropout-1-where.md`, lines 11 and 15).

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/g2-completion-and-course-findings.md` (84-85): “**The dominant non-completion driver is timing:** 69% of minimal-work students didn't start until the last ~6 weeks of the year — out of runway, not quitting. - `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/dropout-4-who.md` (16): “87 of 126 minimal students (69%) did not log their *first activity* in any G2 reading course until the **last ~6 weeks** of the year”

### Fit a test's range to the tails

Fit a test's floor and ceiling, and any items added to an adaptive bank, to where each grade's students sit, not to their average, which can hide either tail. In one population, a grade's bottom quarter averaged 156.6 on the test's score scale, right at the bank's new floor.

A per-grade baseline of a reading assessment's real population found one grade's bottom-quartile mean at RIT 156.6, exactly at the bank's expanded floor, and about a fifth of another grade above RIT 235, which the bank could not yet measure. The package made that table of tails its bank-expansion roadmap in place of an average that hides both edges, and the expansion added items at both ends.

### Fix completion before accuracy

Measure how much of the intended work learners actually finish before tuning accuracy or redesigning content, and when completion is low, fix it and size the course to it first. The course one reading project set out to improve had a median completion of 12.5%.

One redesign of a reading course led with daily 25-minute doses and put completion mechanics before accuracy lifts, noting a cohort floor of 12.5% (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0007-ti-courseplans-repo.qmd`). A later summary of the project's direction calls completion the first problem: the course it set out to improve had a median completion of 12.5%, with about 30% of the intended work done (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0217-team-direction-2026-09-09.qmd`).

### Fix in advance what gives way first

Fix in advance the order in which a time-boxed lesson's parts give way for a slow learner: enrichment and untested items first, never what a later part depends on. One design drops a 2:00 cloze with no test item behind it before a 0:40 device question the test assesses directly, buying three times the time.

A Grade 3 reading lesson design sets a ten-rung drop ladder for a slow child, starting with pure enrichment and then parts another step already covers or no test question stands behind, beside a list of parts never dropped whatever the clock says (`g9/sources/Readventure - Lesson Design and Scaffolding - Updated.docx`, lines 351-418). The never-dropped list includes the taught word, because the independent write cashes it, and that write itself, the only unaided evidence the lesson produces. A revision moved a 2:00 cloze with no test item behind it ahead of a 0:40 device question the test assesses directly, since dropping it buys three times as much time (line 420).

### Flag scores outside the reliable range

Find the ability range over which a test measures reliably, flag every score outside it, and send students below its floor to an instrument built for them. One adaptive reading test measured reliably from 160 to 230 on its score scale, with reliability of at least 0.85, and planned to route readers below its floor to a lower-grade test.

A reading assessment's floor-and-ceiling simulation defines its reliable range as the abilities where reliability reaches 0.85, citing the testing standards' requirement to document the score range within which valid inferences can be made; on the full bank that range ran from RIT 160 to 230. Its score reports carry an above, within or below reliable-range flag, and students below the bank's floor are to go to the official lower-grade instrument rather than be measured past it. At the top, the package added harder items instead.

### Flag the node the graph lacks

When a text presupposes an idea no knowledge-graph node holds, flag the gap rather than force it onto the nearest node, since no check of the graph can see it.

A protocol for placing reading texts on the components of a knowledge graph asks, at its confirm step, whether a text's operation presupposes a mental model that exists in no node, such as that a text has a structure independent of its topic, or that stated and true are different properties. If it does, the step records a graph gap, with the proposed node, why it is load-bearing and which texts surface it, instead of pinning the assumption to the nearest existing component. The protocol's reason is that its deterministic validator checks only the graph it is given, so it cannot catch this class of error by construction; only the confirm step can.

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/_archive/2026-08-13-consolidation/tmp-g5-r8-src-scripts.tar.gz` (scripts/lane-tools/kc-placement/placement-protocol.md inside it) (76-80): “- Missing-conceptual-prerequisite check: does this text's operation presuppose a mental model that exists in NO graph node (e.g. "a text has a structure independent of its topic", "stated and true are different properties")? If yes, do NOT force the assumption onto the nearest existing KC -- flag a GRAPH GAP (proposed node, why it is load-bearing, which texts surface it)”
- `grade3-reading/_archive/2026-08-13-consolidation/tmp-g5-r8-src-scripts.tar.gz` (scripts/lane-tools/kc-placement/placement-protocol.md inside it) (80-81): “The validator cannot catch this class of error by construction”

If yes, do NOT force the assumption onto the nearest existing KC -- flag a GRAPH GAP”

### Frame a gain against normal growth

Judge any gain against the growth that students with the same starting score, grade and weeks of instruction make anyway, which is small for stronger students in later grades. At or above the 50th percentile in grades 6 and up, expected growth on one widely used test flattens toward 1–2 points.

Two course designs in one program, for Grade 7 reading and Grade 7–8 prealgebra, carry the same caveat relayed from a recap: at the 50th percentile and above in grades 6 and up, expected growth on the outside test flattens toward 1–2 points. The reading design says its projections must be framed against that lower base rate or they will look inflated, under its rule to predict direction, not magnitude, before an in-cohort pilot; the prealgebra design says to frame pilot expectations accordingly.

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-reading/brainlifts/v0.1.md` (40): “at the 50th percentile and above in grades 6+, expected MAP growth flattens toward 1–2 points — G7 projections must be framed against that lower base rate, or they'll look inflated.”

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7g8-prealgebra/brainlifts/v0.1.md` (44): “at ≥50th percentile in 6+, expected MAP growth flattens to 1–2 points — frame pilot expectations accordingly.”

- `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/MAP_PROXY_VALIDITY_CASE.md` (25): “it controls for starting ability and asks whether the student grew more or less than expected”

### Grade labels differ between school systems

Before borrowing standards, texts or materials across school systems, check what each year or grade label means there, since the same number can name different ages. England's Year 9 is normally ages 13–14, while US Grade 9 is typically ages 14–15.

Curriculum notes comparing four frameworks for a course whose own specification calls it both Grade 9 and Year 9 (`g9/library/text/L9b6d99.txt`, lines 1 and 4) open with the rule not to merge year labels or frameworks (`g9/library/collections/codex-2026-10-02-curriculum-research/GRADE9-CURRICULUM-OPTIONS.md`, line 5). England's Year 9 is normally ages 13–14 and within Key Stage 3, so it is not the age-equivalent label for US Grade 9, typically ages 14–15 (lines 7-9). A second note, on pandemic-era cases, repeats that the labels should not be treated as interchangeable (`g9/library/collections/codex-2026-10-02-curriculum-research/COVID-ERA-TEACHING-EVIDENCE.md`, line 21).

### Guard every path that writes content

Run blocking content checks on every path that writes content, hand edits included, and roll back any write that fails them. Before its direct-edit path was guarded, one course's rework reintroduced 5 misconception phrasings, caught only by a manual sweep.

A Grade 3 reading course's science misconception gate, as its re-approval package's compliance log records, guarded regeneration: a regenerated lesson whose truth-asserting text still held a Tier-1 (absolute-prohibition) phrase failed and, if the phrase outlasted refinement, was discarded and rolled back. The direct-edit path was not guarded at first, so a rework of the teaching moves done by direct edit reintroduced 5 Tier-1 phrasings, which a manual sweep caught and fixed. An edit guard then snapshotted each file, applied the edit, re-swept it and rolled back to the snapshot if the edit introduced a Tier-1 phrase, so that the sweep blocked shipping on both write paths and a hand edit could no longer leave such a phrase on disk. The check sits on the write itself, rather than on a rerun after the fact.

Quoted:

- `incept-package-hub/.artifacts/source/g3-reading-approval-package.zip` (reapproval-package/sources/MISCONCEPTION-COMPLIANCE-LOG.md inside it) (99): “Earlier in this effort the direct-edit path was NOT guarded, so the teaching-move rework transiently reintroduced 5 Tier-1 phrasings that were caught and fixed by a manual sweep”
- `incept-package-hub/.artifacts/source/g3-reading-approval-package.zip` (reapproval-package/sources/MISCONCEPTION-COMPLIANCE-LOG.md inside it) (97): “**rolls back to the snapshot if the edit introduces a Tier-1 phrase**”
- `incept-package-hub/.artifacts/source/g3-reading-approval-package.zip` (reapproval-package/sources/MISCONCEPTION-COMPLIANCE-LOG.md inside it) (95): “**The Tier-1 sweep is enforced ship-blocking on BOTH write paths:**”
- `incept-package-hub/.artifacts/source/g3-reading-approval-package.zip` (reapproval-package/sources/MISCONCEPTION-COMPLIANCE-LOG.md inside it) (96): “a regenerated lesson whose truth-asserting text contains a Tier-1 phrase fails the PASS condition”
- `incept-package-hub/.artifacts/source/g3-reading-approval-package.zip` (reapproval-package/sources/MISCONCEPTION-COMPLIANCE-LOG.md inside it) (97): “so a hand-edit cannot leave a Tier-1 phrasing on disk either”

Against: One incident in one course; the log reports no later edit that the guard rolled back, so how often it fires is unmeasured.

### Hide no poor results

Tie every piece of work to its student, content and attempt, and show results openly, poor ones included.

The delivery platform the reading project builds for makes this a non-negotiable for every app: the platform must be able to attribute work to student, content and attempt, results are surfaced to students and families, and apps cannot hide poor performance (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0032-principles.qmd`). Apps that fail to emit the required learning signals are not eligible for integration (the same file).

### Hide the rules from the quality pass

Score generated material for rule-following and for quality in separate blind passes, and keep the generation rules out of the quality pass.

The frozen review protocol of an experiment comparing generated Grade 3 reading material gives scorers packets with random IDs and never shows them the arm, model, prompt, cost or other scorers' labels. It splits scoring into a rule-fidelity pass, where the task evidence and the obligation and prohibition rubric are visible, and a holistic-quality pass, where the task evidence and quality rubric are visible but the rules the material was made under are not. The protocol section gives no reason for hiding the rules from the quality pass.

### Hold a lesson's load steady

Count every moment that asks a learner to respond against a target budget for the lesson, and pair any addition that stays with a deletion. One checklist sets about 31 answer moments per lesson as the target and records about 55 as a breach.

The reading project's QC checklist counts discrete answer moments, clozes and your-turn beats included, rather than questions, with about 31 as what it calls the proven target and about 55 as the documented breach (`grade3-reading/artifacts/AlphaRead-QC-Checklist-v2-2026-09-04.md`, B15). A curriculum adherence audit of four lessons judged every page added beyond the design under a conservation rule, in which an addition that stays pairs with a deletion (`grade3-reading/artifacts/curriculum-adherence-2026-09-24/REPORT.md`), and its critic noted 11 added pages with no design basis in one lesson alone (`grade3-reading/artifacts/curriculum-adherence-2026-09-24/CRITIC.md`). Checks that interrupt every paragraph become compliance theater.

### Identify a standard by its full place

Identify a standard by its full place in the curriculum, not by its code alone, and return every match, because one code can name several standards. One curriculum had 284 duplicate standard codes and another had 311.

Standard codes are not unique within a curriculum: the same code can appear in several subjects or courses, which was verified empirically at 284 duplicate standard codes in one curriculum and 311 in another. The curriculum service therefore looks items up with ancestry filters and returns a list of all matches, and its index keeps a list for each code.

Quoted:

- `shadow-curriculum/plans/curriculum-api-decisions.md` (260): “The same `standard_id` can appear in multiple subjects/courses”
- `shadow-curriculum/plans/curriculum-api-decisions.md` (260): “This was verified empirically — CC has 284 duplicate standard IDs, AP has 311.”
- `shadow-curriculum/plans/curriculum-api-decisions.md` (262): “**Decision:** Node-centric API with `target_level` + `ancestry` filters. Returns a list of all matches.”
- `shadow-curriculum/plans/curriculum-api-plan.md` (697): “The value is a list because IDs are not unique within a curriculum.”

Against: The evaluator's transition plan does the opposite: '4. **Multiple results from /fetch** -- Ancestry filtering minimizes this. If multiple results still appear, pick the first one.' (shadow-bench/plans/02-curriculum-api-transition-plan.md line 302), and when nothing is found it retries without the course: '2. If that returns 0 results or fails, retry with `{curriculum, subject}` only (drop course)' (line 80).

### Identity and place from the curriculum map

Take each unit's and lesson's identity and place from the curriculum map, confirm it before authoring, check the content against it before submission, and never fix a mismatch by renaming. One course's units came from a nine-unit draft while the curriculum map it was meant to implement has fourteen.

A visual readiness audit of a Grade 5 course turned up a curriculum identity issue: its units came from a specification of nine units and 55 lessons rather than the supplied fourteen-unit map, and the audit held that its page fixes remain valid evidence about the pages but do not establish alignment, and that the repair is reconciling content, not renaming units (`grade3-reading/visual-findings-2026-09-07/review-readiness/curriculum-alignment/README.md`, lines 9, 27, 35 and 37). A later source audit found a Grade 4 unit built on an internal design that differs from its supplied map, and warned that correcting only the unit title would conceal the mismatch (`grade3-reading/visual-findings-2026-09-08/all-grades-source-audit/GRADE4.md`, line 48). In a Grade 3 course a lesson was written into another lesson's slot because story order was taken as slot authority; it looked coherent in the wrong place and its identity flowed into audio and route paths, so identity now comes from the pinned curriculum graph and is rechecked at the source, build, route and asset layers (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans-wiki/Peter-Pan-Quality-Case-Study-2026-08-24.md`, lines 82-93; `grade3-reading/curriculum-gen/.agent/AGENT.md`, lines 48-50). The Grade 5 rebuild's method calls for a curriculum-identity gate before authoring and a content-to-map check before submission, and, after reused lesson IDs carried unrelated completion and art into replacement lessons, requires a curriculum revision to change identities across progress, session state, unit introductions and asset fallbacks (`grade3-reading/visual-findings-2026-09-07/review-readiness/curriculum-alignment/rebuild/methodology/README.md`, line 44; `grade3-reading/visual-findings-2026-09-07/review-readiness/curriculum-alignment/rebuild/methodology/INTEGRATION-LESSONS.md`, line 15).

### Improve without losing what works

Improve a lesson by fixing flawed parts in place or adding new ones, never by deleting what passed, and rerun a guard on each protected strength after every change.

The reading course's quality standard has a strength-preservation item: improvement never flattens or deletes behaviour that already benefits learners, and each guard on a proven strength is rerun on the changed bytes and must pass an equivalence-or-better test (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/versions/2.0.0/GOLDEN-CHECKLIST.qmd`, line 33). Its refinement workflow treats the source course as the content floor: a refined clone adds compliance, delivery, assessment and evidence layers without cutting source content, and a missing source id fails the build (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/source-course-refinement.qmd`, lines 5 and 47). The course's response to one review round opened with what was landing well, marked keep and do not break. What is protected is what reviews explicitly liked and the verified decisions nearby, so a change that drops or weakens one fails its guard.

Quoted:

### Intervals over clusters of shared material

When items share a prompt or source, compute confidence intervals over those clusters, since repeated material makes a sample look more precise than it is.

The same AP evaluation contract gives repeated prompt or source clusters a cluster-bootstrap interval, so that duplicated substrate cannot create fake precision. Records built on one prompt or one source are not independent draws, so an interval that counts each as its own observation comes out narrower than the evidence allows.

Quoted:

- `grade3-reading/_archive/2026-08-13-consolidation/apush-corpus-hardening-20260731-tip.tar.gz` (apush/docs/INCEPTBENCH-EVALUATION-CONTRACT.md inside it) (118-119): “Repeated prompt or source clusters also receive a cluster-bootstrap interval so duplicated substrate cannot create fake precision.”

Against: The contract was frozen as a design and never run: an AP checkpoint records that no run had been executed for that hand-off (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0170-apush-deliverable-shape-user-pause-checkpoint.qmd`, line 64).

### Isolated gains may not stack

Gains from small isolated tests don't simply add up and can reverse once combined, so re-measure the full combination on fresh items, one change at a time. Two prompt changes that lifted small paired pilots by 60 and 75 points cut one item type's fresh first-try rate from 80% to 76% once stacked.

Two prompt changes, a stated time period at the start of the stem and an easy difficulty label, each lifted a hand-made paired pilot, by 60 points on 5 pairs and by 75 points on 4 (`icloud-work/aptraining/Cheater/exploits/EXPLOIT-006-period-anchor.md`; `icloud-work/aptraining/Cheater/exploits/EXPLOIT-007-difficulty-downgrade.md`). Once stacked into the working prompts, first-try rates on fresh topics fell for three item types, from 88% to 76%, 79% to 75% and 80% to 76% (`icloud-work/aptraining/Cheater/exploits/EXPLOIT-007-difficulty-downgrade.md`; `icloud-work/aptraining/Cheater/from_cheater/SINGLE_IB_GRADE_SURVIVAL_GUIDE.md`). Add or remove one change at a time, and keep only changes whose removal measurably hurts.

The pilot had four items, so its lift may have been noise rather than a real effect that other changes undid. Per-type counts rest on 3 to 5 items from one seed, and the source puts the noise floor at about one item per type at 15 items. The directive set as a whole was worth +8 passes (15/25 to 23/25), so additions don't generally hurt, and the losing bundle also ran through repair routes that bypassed its instructions.

### Judge a diagnostic by its routing

Judge a diagnostic by whether students who follow its routing learn faster, and stop testing once the next item is worth less than the study time it takes. A 70% confident finding that a chapter is a gap is enough to route a student, and 10 more items to reach 90% may not be worth the study time.

The diagnostic guide in the reading project's knowledge base treats a diagnostic as a routing decision, not a measurement: it is good if students who follow its recommendations learn more efficiently than students who don't, so a rough but fast one can beat a precise but slow one (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0154-diagnostic-assessment-brainlift.qmd`). Since time spent testing is time not spent studying, it tests only until the expected value of the next item for routing falls below that of spending the time studying. The course's routing contract says diagnostics route study under uncertainty and are not grades (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0164-g3-v2-feedback-agent-routing.qmd`).

Against: The guide is design doctrine; no diagnostic in these sources has yet been judged by how fast its students learn (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0154-diagnostic-assessment-brainlift.qmd`).

### Judge by hours to a verified outcome

Judge material by the time students need to reach a verified outcome, not by time spent, which measures presence rather than learning.

The delivery platform's quality bar for apps counts efficiency as fewer hours to reach the same verified outcome (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0026-evaluating-apps.qmd`). Its effort metric exists because tracking time measures presence, not learning, and tracking accuracy ignores how much work was done, so it combines effort with proof (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0030-xp-system.qmd`).

Against: none found

### Judge the lesson, not only its items

Passing items don't make a good set, lesson or course, so judge each whole on how its parts work together, taking item verdicts as given, never by adding them up. One evaluator run rated 529 of 1026 items superior but 73 of 76 lessons inferior.

One evaluator run over 76 cloned reading lessons rated 529 of their 1026 items superior but 73 of the 76 lessons inferior, and 65 of the 76 scored exactly 0 on not repeating themselves. The reading course passed its item-level evaluations but not the holistic course-level one, and a later project note says new metrics are needed to assess lesson sequencing. Judge their sequence, coverage, difficulty ramp and balance, with several lessons in view.

Against: the scores are one run of a model judge, and the zeros on multi-passage lessons say more about how the evaluation was packaged than about the content. The lesson-level verdicts are the same evaluator's, not a person's, and the notes mark the figure internal-only (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/HOTBUCKET.md`). At lesson level the evaluator does average item scores when there is no shared passage: '- _assemble_no_stimulus_result() returns item scores + avg overall' (shadow-bench, git commit 7b5da6e, line 9). The manual cover for cross-lesson defects is untested: 'assigned, not covered' (shadow-bench/docs/brainlift.md line 147). The set specification does not count a shared format as repetition: "- Same question format (MCQ) applied to different concepts" (`icloud-work/incept/inceptbench/docs/MCQ_SET_PASS_SPEC.md`, line 203); these stems were near-copies, not one format applied to different concepts. Per-item verdicts vary between runs (see verdicts-vary), and the lesson rubric folds them in by threshold: a lesson fails factual accuracy only when more than 20% of its items do (`lesson_bundle/evaluation.txt` line 140), so a lesson with a few wrong items can pass, against the rule that a wrong key or wrong fact voids an item.

<sub>method · stage: measure · measurement, sequence, evaluation · universal · from ap, g3 · measured · held · found in [2026-10-12-3-round-2](../research/2026-10-12-3-round-2/), [2026-10-12-4-deep-sweep](../research/2026-10-12-4-deep-sweep/), [2026-10-12-5-full-crawl](../research/2026-10-12-5-full-crawl/)</sub>

### Judge the set as well as each item

Check a bank, form or course as a set as well as item by item: find repeats, near-duplicates and items that give away, prime or contradict one another. 65 of 76 lesson bundles scored exactly 0 on a quality judge's check for repeats.

A quality judge's bundle-level check found repeats inside most lessons: non-repetitiveness averaged 0.14, and 65 of 76 bundles scored exactly 0 on it (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0083-clone-lessons-inceptbench-results-2026-07-02-eval-summary.qmd`). A Grade 3 course passed that judge's item-level evaluation but not its holistic course-level one (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0076-coe-catchup-2026-06-30.qmd`), and a live test form whose items were bound to an unrelated passage was recorded as the kind of defect that passes item evals and fails the course eval (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0234-misc-artifacts-gate-eval-checks-recovery.qmd`). In one review round a single word pair cracked the usage checks on two forms (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0211-peter-pan-reviewer-round-2708.qmd`), and the project's routing rules make answer position, option length, distractor function, enemy items, blueprints and independent cold review obligations of the form (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0164-g3-v2-feedback-agent-routing.qmd`). Check answer positions, option lengths, key spread and coverage across the set, and keep parallel forms disjoint.

### Judge the whole screen as it changes

Check each screen as a whole at each moment, and withdraw used scaffolding once the learner succeeds, because correct parts can add up to clutter or two asks at once. After one correct answer, a guided-practice screen showed nine stacked blocks with the proof line printed three times.

A Grade 3 reading build's BrainLift records two defects on one guided-practice screen: a correct tap left nine stacked blocks with the proof line printed three times, and, after that fix was merged, a spoken stretch question and a say-back card asked different things at the same moment. Neither was a bug in any component; both were the sum of correct components, and the build's rules call the second defect simultaneity, not existence, so the stretch was kept but split off and printed quieter. Ruled-out options, hints and duplicate success boxes now withdraw on success, and a declutter gate holds the screen at 630 assertions.

### Keep each source's detail when merging

When similar standards or sources are merged into one shared unit, keep each one's specific detail inside it, because a merged abstract description is too vague to drive lessons.

The curriculum BrainLift describes an attempt to build one common graph for social studies by merging similar-looking standards from different states into unified nodes: the result was flattened abstractions that lost the specificity needed for teaching, too vague to generate good instruction (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback1/Curriculum & Knowledge BrainLift.md`). The reading project's curriculum reference turned this into a rule: preserve state-specific detail inside nodes and never merge into abstract common nodes (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/train-teacher/references/curriculum-architecture.md`).

Quoted:

### Keep every sentence, however short

A check that matches answers to the text must keep every sentence that carries a content word, however short. A minimum of 10 characters dropped a one-word sentence of exactly 10 and made a correctly keyed answer look unsupported.

A content audit for Grade 3 reading lessons splits each story into sentences to check that a keyed answer is supported by the text. An earlier minimum length of 10 characters silently dropped one-word sentences, which is where that prose puts its key words, and made a correctly keyed answer look unsupported; the splitter now keeps every sentence that carries a content word (`shadow/content-eval/SKILL.md`).

### Keep simulated review perspectives apart

Run each simulated review perspective in its own process, blind to the others' prompts and results until code combines them. One preflight ran three simulated perspectives against one lesson, each in a fresh process.

A Grade 5 lesson preflight runs three isolated simulated characters against one exact learner artifact, one fresh process per character, and none receives another's prompt or result; cross-character visibility is forbidden until deterministic aggregation. Its contract forbids numeric scores and any whole-course claim from one lesson, and sets that human sign-off may not be minted by simulation.

### Keep standards free of pipeline details

Keep pipeline and data-format instructions out of a curriculum's descriptions, and don't remove a real constraint from a standard unless it is kept somewhere else.

A procedure for reviewing edits to a curriculum data store, written from real reviews, sets as its goal never approving an edit that contradicts itself or strips a constraint without a replacement (`shadow/curriculum/.agents/skills/curriculum-pr-review/SKILL.md` line 10). Edits that strip internal field names and typing rules from standards are approved only after checking the repository's schemas: a typing rule that isn't in them was a leaked pipeline detail, and removing it is correct (lines 47 and 143). A removed rule is also fine when the standard's own examples already encode it (line 142).
